getRootPane().setDefaultButton(okButton);
  • You can also set the default enter button in a JFrame by using JFrame's getRootPane() method and JRootPane's setDefaultButton() method.

Project 11 - Word Builder

Word Builder is a word game in which the player gets points by creating words from letter tiles arranged in a grid of 8 rows and 12 columns. Each tile can be used only once and only if it is in the top row. When a tile is removed from the top row, all the other tiles in the column move up to fill the empty space.

Valid words have at least 3, and no more than 15, letters. Points are calculated by multiplying each letter's point value by the length of the word. The longer the word, the more points earned per letter.

This game comes complete with a dictionary of more than 168,000 words, each having 3 to 15 letters.

Here is a screenshot of the Word Builder game:

Try It - Check If a Word is in the Dictionary

Dictionary will need to check whether a word is in the dictionary. The words in the word lists are in alphabetical order. So if Dictionary finds a word greater than the search word before it finds the search word, the word is not in the dictionary.

String's compareTo() method will compare strings and return an integer. If the integer is less than 0, the first string is less than the second string. If the integer is equal to 0, the strings are equal. If the integer is greater than 0, the first string is greater than the second string.

The words in the word list are all upper case. Dictionary must convert a word to upper case before checking whether the word is in the list.

  7. Create a string called word2, initialized to an empty string.

Key Points and More

  • The dictionary file provided for this program is named enable1_3-15.txt. It contains all the 3 to 15-letter words from the original dictionary file, enabel1.txt.
    • The name of the file “enable” is an abbreviation for “Enhanced North American Benchmark LExicon”.
    • enable1.txt is a free public domain file, and may be downloaded from many different sites on the web, including http://www.puzzlers.org/dokuwiki/doku.php?id=solving:wordlists:about:start&s=word%20list.
    • For more information, see the comments from the author of enable1.txt at http://www.puzzlers.org/dokuwiki/doku.php?id=solving:wordlists:about:enable_readme.
  • You can use String's compareTo() method to compare strings. compareTo() returns an integer:
    • less than 0 if the first string is less than the second string.
    • equal to 0 if the strings are equal.
    • greater than 0 if the first string is greater than the second string.
  • For example, to check if the value of the string myName comes before the value of the string yourName alphabetically, use:
if (myName.compareTo(yourName)<0) {
  • The compareTo() method compares upper and lower case letters differently. If you want code to ignore the case of the letters, either convert both string values to upper case or lower case, or use String's compareToIgnoreCase() method.

Key Points and More

  • To draw a string, use Graphics' drawString() method with the string and the x and y coordinates of where to draw the string on the Graphics object.
  • Whereas other Graphics' draw methods used the top edge of the drawing as the y coordinate, drawString() uses the baseline of the text as the y coordinate. For example, the string “Happy Birthday” has a baseline at the bottom edge of the letter “H”. The letter “y” falls below the baseline of the word. Therefore if you want to put a string inside a rectangle, you cannot simply use the same y coordinate for the drawRect() method and the drawString() method.
  • Use font metrics to get information about a string that depends on its font. To create a FontMetrics object, use JPanel's getFontMetrics() method, with the intended font as the parameter value.
  • Use FontMetrics' stringWidth() method to calculate what a string's width will be when drawn with FontMetrics' font. For example, to create a font metrics called fm, for a font called font, and then get the width of the string “Happy Birthday” in that font, use:
FontMetrics fm = new FontMetrics(font);
int stringWidth = fm.stringWidth("Happy Birthday");
  • To center a string horizontally within a rectangle requires three steps: 1) Divide the width of the rectangle in half to find the center of the rectangle. 2) Subtract half of the string width from the center of the rectangle. 3) Add that result to the x coordinate of the rectangle. For example, for a rectangle drawn at coordinates x and y, with width w and height h, to center a string whose width is stringWidth in that rectangle, calculate the x coordinate of the string like this:
int stringX = x + w/2 - stringWidth/2;
  • To right align a string within a rectangle requires two steps: 1) Add the width of the rectangle to the x coordinate of the rectangle. 2) Subtract the width of the string. For example, for a rectangle drawn at coordinates x and y, with width w and height h, to right align a string whose width is stringWidth in that rectangle, calculate the x coordinate of the string like this:
int stringX = x + w - stringWidth;
  • You can also get the height of a string drawn in a given font. Do so by first using FontMetrics' getStringBounds() method, with the string and the Graphics object as the parameter values. getStringBounds() will return a Rectangle2D object, with which you can call getHeight() to get the string's height. A string's height is not used in any of the programs in this book.

Key Points and More

  • Depending on the layout chosen, packing a window may pack components closer together than you would like. You can change the space between components.
  • To add space between components in a BoxLayout, create an invisible rigid component or an invisible glue component.
  • A rigid component will ensure an exact amount of space is inserted between the components.
  • A glue component inserts space that will stretch if the panel has extra space to fill. Think of glue components as being “gooey” like glue.
  • Create a rigid component by using Box's createRigidArea() method with a Dimension. You can use 0 for either the width or height of the Dimension if you want BoxLayout to use the panel's width or height for that dimension. For example, if infoPanel uses BoxLayout and if you want to create an invisible component called spacer 10 pixels wide and as tall as infoPanel and then add spacer to infoPanel, use:
Dimension size = new Dimension(10, 0);
Component spacer = new Box.createRigidArea(size);
infoPanel.add(spacer);
  • Create a glue component by using Box's createGlue() method with no parameter values. To add equal amount of space between multiple components in a row or column, insert a glue component between each component. For example, if infoPanel uses BoxLayout and you want an equal amount of space inserted before, between, and after components named yes and no, use:
infoPanel.add(Box.createGlue());
infoPanel.add(yes);
infoPanel.add(Box.createGlue());
infoPanel.add(no);
infoPanel.add(Box.createGlue());
  • You can also use Box's createHorizontalGlue() or createVerticalGlue() if you only want the glue component to stretch in one direction.
  • You'll be adding glue components in a later lesson.
  • To add space between components in a GridLayout, call GridLayout's constructor with four parameter values: the number of rows, the number of columns, the horizontal gap, and the vertical gap. The horizontal gap is the space between columns and the vertical gap is the space between rows. For example, to create a grid layout of 3 rows and 4 columns, with a gap of 10 pixels between columns and 5 pixels between rows, and put the layout on a panel called tilePanel, use:
tilePanel.setLayout(new GridLayout(3, 4, 10, 5));
  • FlowLayout puts a 5 pixel space between components by default. To use different spacing between components of a FlowLayout, call FlowLayout's constructor with three parameter values: the alignment of the row of components, the components' horizontal gap, and the components' vertical gap. For example, to create a flow layout with the row components right aligned, with a horizontal gap of 10 and a vertical gap of 5, and put the layout on a panel called optionsPanel, use:
optionsPanel.setLayout(new FlowLayout(FlowLayout.RIGHT, 10, 5));
  • To add space between components in a BorderLayout, call BorderLayout's constructor with two parameter values: the horizontal gap and vertical gap. For example, to create a border layout with a horizontal gap of 10 pixels and a vertical gap of 5 pixels, and put the layout on a panel called mainPanel, use:
mainPanel.setLayout(new BorderLayout(10, 5));

Key Points and More

  • Date is actually a combination of date and time. Getting the current date checks the clock on the computer and gets the date and time to the nearest millisecond.
  • To get the current date, create a new Date object by calling Date's constructor with no parameter values. Note, import java.util.Date.
  • To convert the value from a Date object to a string, the Date object must first be formatted with a date formatter. The date formatter that is easiest to use is the SimpleDateFormat. Use the following symbols to create a string that shows the format you choose. (These symbols are the symbols you are most likely to use. Other symbols are available, and so is other information one can get from the date, such as day of week, day of year, and more. Refer to the Java API for more details.)
    • y - year
    • M - month in year
    • d - day in month
    • a - am or pm
    • H - hour in day (0-23)
    • k - hour in day (1-24)
    • K - hour in am/pm (0-11)
    • h - hour in am/pm (1-12)
    • m - minute in hour
    • s - second in minute
    • S - millisecond
  • Repeat the symbol in the format string for the minimum number of digits to use. The exception is the month. “M” and “MM” will restrict the month to a minimum of one or two digits. “MMM” will abbreviate the month name. “MMMM” will display the entire month name.
  • After defining a SimpleDateFormat, call SimpleDateFormat's format() method to convert the value from a Date object into a string with that format.
  • For example, to format a Date object called date, whose value is July 4, 2015, 2:15pm, to print like this: “07/04/15”, use:
DateFormat format1 = new SimpleDateFormat("MM/dd/yy");
System.out.println(format1.format(date));
  • To format the same date to print like this: “July 4, 2015 14:15”, use
DateFormat format2 = new SimpleDateFormat("MMMM d yyyy HH:mm");
System.out.println(format2.format(date));

Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window

If you allow the window to be resizable, a user might change the size of the window, which should probably cause the program to resize the window's contents by the same relative amount.

A component listener would be notified if the user dragged the edge of the window. A window state listener would be notified if the user maximized or minimized the window, or returned the window to normal state.

Try It - Listen for the Window to be Resized

WordBuilder will need to respond to events when the window changes size.

  1. In the listeners section of initGUI(), add a component listener to call resizeWindow() when the window's frame is dragged to a new size. (Hint: use JFrame's addComponentListener() method, with a new ComponentAdapter object as the parameter value. In the ComponentAdapter, add a public method called componentResized(). componentResized() should have one parameter, a ComponentEvent, and return nothing. In componentResized(), call resizeWindow().)
  2. Add a window state listener to call resizeWindow() when the window is maximized, or returned to its original state. (Hint: use JFrame's addWindowStateListener() method, with a new WindowStateListener object as the parameter value. In the WindowStateListener, add a public method called windowStateChanged(). windowStateChanged() should have one parameter, a WindowEvent, and return nothing. In windowStateChanged(), call resizeWindow().)

Note: the code will have a syntax error because resizeWindow() doesn't exist yet.

Key Points and More

  • To listen for a change in window size, add a component listener to the JFrame.
  • To add a component listener to a window, use JFrame's addComponentListener() method.
  • To add a component listener, add a ComponentAdapter object instead of a ComponentListener object. ComponentAdapter extends ComponentListener, so may be used anywhere ComponentListener is allowed. But much less code is required for a ComponentAdapter than for a ComponentListener.
  • If you want a new ComponentAdapter to recognize when a component is resized, add a public method to the ComponentAdapter called componentResized(), with one parameter, a ComponentEvent, and return nothing. For example, to add a component listener to a JFrame that calls resize() when the window is resized, use:
addComponentListener(new ComponentAdapter() {
	public void componentResized(ComponentEvent e) {
		resize();
	}
});
  • To listen for the window being maximized, minimized, or returned to normal state, add a window state listener to the JFrame.
  • To add a window state listener to a window, use JFrame's addWindowStateListener() method.
  • To add a window state listener, add a new WindowStateListener with a public method called windowStateChanged() that takes one parameter, a WindowEvent, and returns nothing. For example, to add a window state listener to JFrame that calls resize() when the window state is changed, use:
addWindowStateListener(new WindowStateListener() {
	public void windowStateChanged(WindowEvent e) {
		resize();
	}
});
  • Whenever a window is resized, calculate how much the window was resized, then resize the components the same relative amount.
    • First get the new size of a panel that changed size, using JPanel's getWidth() and getHeight() methods.
    • Calculate each component's new size, based on what percentage of the panel the component should use. You might use the percentage change in width, height, or both. Set the new preferred size of each component.

Key Points and More

  • Get the window's location with JFrame's getLocation() method, which returns a Point for the upper left corner of the window. Get the integer x and y coordinates of that point by using Point's x and y static instance variables.
  • Get the window's size with JFrame's getSize() method, which returns a Dimension. Get the integer width and height of that dimension by using Dimension's width and height static instance variables.
  • Get the window's state with JFrame's getExtendedState() method. getExtendedState() will return an integer whose value will be either ICONIFIED if the window is minimized, MAXIMIZED_BOTH if the window is maximized, or NORMAL if the window is neither minimize nor maximized.
  • Set the window's location with JFrame's setLocation() method, passing in the x and y coordinates for the upper left corner of the window.
  • Set the window's size with JFrame's setSize() method, passing in the width and height for the window.
  • Set the window's state with JFrame's setExtendedState() method, passing in JFrame's ICONIFIED, MAXIMIZED_BOTH, or NORMAL variable.
  • To listen for the window being opened, closed, newly active, or no longer active, add a window listener to the window using JFrame's addWindowListener() method.
  • To add a window listener, add a new WindowAdapter with any of the following public methods, each with one parameter, a WindowEvent, and each with nothing returned.
    • windowActivated - runs when the window becomes active.
    • windowClosed - runs when the window has been disposed.
    • windowClosing - runs when the program user closes the window, using the window's close button.
    • windowDeactivated - runs when the window becomes no longer active.
    • windowDeiconified - runs when the window returns to normal state after being minimized.
    • windowIconified - runs when the window is minimized.
    • windowOpened - runs when the window becomes visible.
  • To add a window listener, add a WindowAdapter object instead of a WindowListener object. WindowAdapter extends WindowListener, so may be used anywhere WindowListener is allowed. But much less code is required for a WindowAdapter than for a WindowListener.
  • For example, to add a window state listener to JFrame that calls save() when the window is closed, use:
addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() {
	public void windowClosed(WindowEvent e) {
		save();
	}
});

Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File

So far you've been told that you must always keep required files in the same folder as the exported JAR file. You must always do that if the program will ever need to make changes to the file. However, files that will not be changed could be placed in the JAR file, thus ensuring they're kept with the JAR file.

Try It - Export the Program and Its Files

If you export a program, any additional files you want included in the JAR file must be placed in the project's src folder.

You have completed the Word Builder program.

Run It

Double clicking the exported JAR file name should run the program with the same results as it had before.

Key Points and More

  • Files that must be updated by the program or that you want the program user to access directly for any other reason, must be read with a file reader and kept in the same folder as the JAR file after the program is exported.
  • Files that are only read by the program may be exported into the JAR file, thus keeping the file with the JAR file. However, you cannot read the file in the JAR file using a file reader. You must instead read the file using an input stream.
  • In preparation for getting your program to read from the input stream, copy the file into your project's bin folder.
    • Eclipse occasionally rebuilds the project's bin folder, which would remove the files you copied there. You must then copy the files back into the bin folder in order to run the program from within Eclipse.
  • To create an InputStream object, first get the class of the object that will read the file using Object's getClass() method. Then get the InputStream from that class with Class's getResourceAsStream() method, using the name of the file. If the file is in your bin folder, put a “/” at the front of the file name. Note, Java uses a forward slash, “/”, in file paths and Windows uses a backslash, “\” , in file paths. If the file is in a subfolder of your bin folder, put a “/” and the name of the subfolder in front of the file name. For example, to create a BufferedReader object called in to read a file called smiley.gif as an input stream from your project's bin\images folder, use:
InputStream input = getClass().getResourceAsStream("/images/smiley.gif");
BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(input));
  • When you're ready to export your program to a JAR file, copy the file, and any subfolders it was contained in, from the project's bin folder into the project's src folder. The file will then automatically be placed in the same subfolder in the JAR file when the program is exported. For example, the above smiley.gif file should be copied to both bin\images and src\images.
  • After you copy the files to the project's src folder, refresh the project in Eclipse, so Eclipse can find the file for exporting the project.
    • To refresh a project in Eclipse, right click on the project in Package Explorer and choose Refresh.
    • After refreshing a project, you should see the extra files listed in the src folder of the project in Eclipse's Package Explorer.

Project 12 - Image Resizer

Image Resizer isn't exactly a game, but a tool that will help you create appropriately sized images for games. You'll be able to resize an image to a new size while keeping the same width to height ratio, or crop an image by selecting a rectangular area of the image. For example, you could use the Image Resizer program to make your own 200 pixel wide and 200 pixel high image for the Sliding Tiles program.

Here is a screenshot of the Image Resizer program:

Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars

In this lesson you'll create a toolbar with images, buttons, and input fields.

Try It - Do Initial Setup for ImageResizer

Start writing the Image Resizer program.

  1. Create a new Java project called Image Resizer and add project My Components to Image Resizer.
  2. Create a new package called ___________._____________.imageresizer in the project.
  3. Create a new class called ImageResizer, with superclass JFrame and with a stub for main().
  4. Use Quick Fix to add a private static final long instance variable called serialVersionUID, set to 1L.
  5. Add an ImageResizer constructor with no parameters. In the constructor:
    1. Call initGUI().
    2. Set the window's title to “Image Resizer”, pack the window, center the window, make the window visible, and set the window to exit when closed.
  6. Create a new private method called initGUI(). It should take no parameters and return nothing. In initGUI(), add a TitleLabel with text “Image Resizer” to the top of the window.
  7. Add code to main() to use the cross platform look and feel and to create a new ImageResizer object on the event queue.

Listing 12-1, from ImageResizer.java

package annette.godtland.imageresizer;
 
import java.awt.BorderLayout;

Key Points and More

  • Add a toolbar to a window by creating a new JToolBar object with JToolBar's constructor. Use JPanel's or JFrame's add() method to add a toolbar to a panel or window, respectively.
  • The default JToolBar object is floatable. If you click and drag the handle in the toolbar you can drop the toolbar along a different edge of the window to attach the toolbar to that edge of the window. Or you can drop the toolbar anywhere else to detach it from the window and use the toolbar like a modal dialog.
  • Add components to a toolbar the same way you add components to any other panel.
  • Toolbars often use image buttons instead of text buttons. To create an image button, call the JButton constructor with an ImageIcon instead of a string.
  • If you use an image instead of a string for a button, you should provide tool tip text for the button. Tool tip text displays when the program user rests the mouse on the button. To add tool tip text, use JButton's setToolTipText() method, with the string whose value is the text you want displayed.
  • You can also use an image instead of a string for a label. To create an image label, call the JLabel constructor with an ImageIcon instead of a string.
  • If you use images in your toolbar, you should plan to put them in the JAR file if the program is exported. So copy all toolbar image files to your project's bin and src folders and use an input stream to read them.
  • The images used on the toolbar of this program were 16 pixels wide and 16 pixels high.
  • Add action listeners to buttons in the toolbar the same way you've added action listeners to buttons in other containers.
  • You can add separators between different sets of tools on the toolbar by calling JToolBar's addSeparator() method.

Key Points and More

  • To save an image, use ImageIO's write() method, passing these parameter values: a BufferedImage object, the image format, and a File object in which to save the image. The format should be entered as a string and may be “jpg”, “png”, “gif”, or “bmp”. For example, to save an image called image as a “.gif” into a file called “icon.gif”, use:
File file = new File("icon.gif");
ImageIO.write(image, "gif", file);
  • If the name the user selects for the file doesn't include an extension, you should add the appropriate extension for him.
  • You should always ask the user if he is sure he wants to replace a file if a file already exists by that name.
  • Because the ImageResizer program was written to save images only in the JPEG format, the program used a file filter to only open files with a “.jpg” extension. If you want to, you could change the file filter to open other types of image files and then give the user the option to save the image into the other image formats as well.
  • The JPEG file format is intended to compress an image, to make the file size smaller. If you open an image, and save it with a new name, you should see that the file size of new image is much smaller than the file size of the original image. The new image will be the same relative shape and size, but will be saved as fewer bytes of data. This may reduce the image quality. The more times you save an image in a JPEG file format, the poorer the image quality will be.

Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners

A focus listener can listen for when a field comes into focus or goes out of focus. For example, if a program user types a value into the width field, then moves the cursor out of that field, the field will lose focus and a focus listener on the width field can update the height field to an appropriate value.

Key Points and More

  • To make your program listen for when focus enters or leaves a component, you have to add a focus listener. In this book you add the focus listeners to input fields.
  • To add a focus listener to an input field, use JTextField's addFocusListener() method.
  • To add a focus listener, add a FocusAdapter object instead of a FocusListener object. FocusAdapter extends FocusListener, so may be used anywhere FocusListener is allowed. But much less code is required for a FocusAdapter than for a FocusListener.
  • If you want a new FocusAdapter to recognize when focus enters or leaves a text field, add one of these public methods:
    • focusGained() - will run when focus enters the text field.
    • focusLost() - will run when focus leaves the text field.
  • Each of the above methods must have one parameter, a FocusEvent, and return nothing. For example, to add a focus listener that calls isValid() when focus leaves a field called phoneNumber, use:
phoneNumber.addFocusListener(new FocusAdapter() {
	public void focusLost(FocusEvent e) {
		isValid();
	}
});
  • To get the component that gained or lost its focus, use FocusEvent's getSource() method, then cast the source value to the type of component the listener is defined on. For example, if the focus listener was defined on a JTextField and you wanted to pass the contents of that field to a method called updateRecords() when focus is lost, use:
public void focusLost(FocusEvent e) {
	JTextField field = (JTextField)e.getSource();
	String text = field.getText();
	updateRecords(text);
}

Lesson 12.4 - XOR Mode

Some photos are dark, some are light, most have dark and light areas scattered throughout. How can you choose a drawing color that would show up on all photos?

By setting the drawing color to black, then setting XOR mode to white, Java will choose black or white or some color in between, for every pixel drawn. Java will choose each pixel color, based on the color of the pixel being replaced.

  4. If y is greater than startY then set cropH to y minus startY.
  5. Otherwise:

    2. Set cropY to y.

Key Points and More

  • To draw with a mouse, the program must check where the mouse was clicked and how much the mouse was dragged in each direction.
  • Use a mouse listener to check where the mouse was clicked. Use a mouse motion listener to check how much the mouse was dragged.
  • You already know how to add a mouse listener. To update program variables to the location where the mouse was clicked, use the MouseAdapter's mousePressed() method. Get the x and y coordinates from the mouse event with MouseEvent's getX() and getY() methods. For example, to call a method called beginDraw() with two integer parameter values, x and y coordinates, when the mouse is clicked, use:
addMouseListener(new MouseAdapter() {
	public void mousePressed(MouseEvent e) {
		int x = e.getX();
		int y = e.getY();
		beginDraw(x, y);
	}
});
  • To make your program listen for the mouse being dragged, add a mouse motion listener. In this book you add the mouse motion listeners to panels.
  • Use a mouse motion listener to calculate how much the mouse moved.
  • To add a mouse motion listener to a panel, use JPanel's addMouseMotionListener() method.
  • To add a mouse motion listener, add a MouseMotionAdapter object instead of a MouseMotionListener object. MouseMotionAdapter extends MouseMotionListener, so may be used anywhere MouseMotionListener is allowed. But much less code is required for a MouseMotionAdapter than for a MouseMotionListener.
  • If you want a new MouseMotionAdapter to recognize the mouse being dragged, add the public method mouseDragged(). mouseDragged() must have one parameter, a MouseEvent, and return nothing. mouseDragged() should get the mouse's new x and y coordinates from the mouse event with MouseEvent's getX() and getY() methods. For example, to call a method called redraw() with two integer parameter values, x and y coordinates, when the mouse is dragged, use:
addMouseMotionListener(new MouseMotionAdapter() {
	public void mouseDragged(MouseEvent e) {
		int x = e.getX();
		int y = e.getY();
		redraw(x, y);
	}
});
  • The beginDraw() method should then update instance variables for where the drawing started. The redraw() method should calculate how much the mouse moved from the drawing start coordinates, set instance variables needed by the paintComponent() method to draw to the new coordinates, then call repaint().
  • The mouse drawing examples in this book all create temporary drawings: the previous drawing disappears as the mouse moves. Temporary drawings are implemented by having the paintComponent() method redraw the background every time repaint() is called. Temporary drawings are intentionally used in this book because these projects are best implemented with temporary drawings.
  • If you instead wanted drawings to remain on the panel, such as if you were trying to write a paint program, or continuing to build on a path taken, you could create a BufferedImage object, get its Graphics object, and draw on that like you did in previous projects. Your beginDraw() and redraw() methods could just keep adding to the image. Then paintComponent() would just draw that image to the panel's Graphics object.
    • Why not just draw in paintComponent(), without redrawing the panel's background? That approach would appear to work. However, if the program user minimizes and maximizes the window, or places another window over the top of the window your program displays, then moves the other window away, paintComponent() would not be able to redraw everything that was drawn before. paintComponent() must be able to repaint all the panel's content at any time.

Project 13 - Baker's Dozen Solitaire

Baker's Dozen is a solitaire card game played with a standard deck of 52 cards. All the cards are dealt face up, in four rows of thirteen columns. All kings are moved to the top of the row in which they were dealt. The object of the game is to build four stacks of cards (the foundation stacks) from ace through king, following suit.

Only the cards at the bottom of the columns may be played, and only one card at a time. A card may be moved to a foundation, if the card matches suit and follows upward sequence, or it may be added to the bottom of any other column, if the card follows downward sequence. The suit doesn't matter for moving a card to another column. However, a card may not be played on an empty column.

Here is a screenshot of the Baker's Dozen Solitaire program in progress:

Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images

Drawing on a panel with transparent colors allows background colors to show through. Moving an image on a panel when the image has some transparent colors gives the appearance of moving an irregularly-shaped object instead of a rectangle.

Portable Network Graphic, PNG (file with extension “.png”), is another image file format. But unlike Joint Photographic Experts Group, JPEG format (file with extension “.jpg”), PNG format supports transparent colors.

Try It - Make the Background Transparent

Another improvement would be to make the background transparent instead of green. Then, if a card is moved over a second card, the second card can be seen past the first card's rounded corners. Transparency is allowed in PNG files but not JPEG files. Transparency is set in the alpha value of a color, which is also called the color's alpha channel.

  1. In paintComponent(), change the initialization of image to use the BufferedImage type that allows the additional alpha channel. (Hint: use BufferedImage's TYPE_INT_ARGB variable.)
  2. Change the first color used from GREEN to a fully transparent white color. (Hint: use the Color constructor with four parameter values. Use 0 for red, green, and blue parameter values to create white. Use 0 for the fourth parameter value to make the color fully transparent.)

Try It - Move the Image File so It May Be Read as a Stream

Later, the program will need to be able to read the image file, cards.png, as a stream.

  • Copy the file, cards.png, to the BakersDozen\bin folder of your Java work folder.

Key Points and More

  • Panels always fill a rectangular area. If you want a panel to appear as any other shape, fill the panel's background with a transparent color and draw any shape object over the transparent background.
  • Color has a constructor with four integers: red, green, blue, and alpha channel. The alpha channel sets how transparent to make the color. 0 means totally transparent, 255 means totally opaque (no transparency). For example, to create a color called transparent that's totally transparent, use any values for red, green, and blue and use 0 for the alpha channel, like this:
Color transparent = new Color(100, 220, 55, 0);
  • The previously used file format of JPEG doesn't support transparency. Both GIF and PNG file formats support transparency, but GIF supports only fully transparent or fully opaque cases. PNG supports varying levels of transparency.
  • To save a file with the PNG format, use “png” as the format type for ImageIO's write() method. For example, to save an image called rocketDrawing to a file named “rocket.png” with the PNG format, use:
ImageIo.write(rocketDrawing, "png", new File("rocket.png"));
  • Were you wondering why you created a BufferedImage to draw on, instead of adding a paintComponent() method like you did in so many of the previous classes? The previous classes were all JPanels. No window or user interface was needed for this program. So this program has no components. Therefore, paintComponent() would have no component to paint. To paint something if you have no component, create a BufferedImage object.

Lesson 13.2 - Objects on a Panel

If you want multiple objects painted on a panel, the panel could keep track of where and how to draw each object. However, with class definitions for each of the objects, writing the program is easier if each object keeps track of where and how to draw itself.

Key Points and More

  • Each object should keep track of its x and y coordinates.
  • Each object should have its own draw method with a Graphics parameter on which the object will be drawn.
  • The main panel's paintComponent() method can then draw all of the objects in the panel by passing the panel's Graphics object to each object's draw method.

Lesson 13.3 - Move Objects

To move an object, first draw the object in one location, then erase the object and draw it again in a new location. Repeated in small steps, this approach animates the object. If a mouse is used to move an object, a program can get x and y coordinates from a MouseEvent, and use those coordinates to draw the object being moved.

Key Points and More

  • To drag an object on a panel with the mouse, the object should have:
    • Variables for keeping its x and y coordinates.
    • A method to draw the object at its current x and y coordinates on a given Graphics object.
    • A method that checks if given x and y coordinates are inside the object.
    • A method to set its x and y coordinates to given x and y values and then repaint the object.
    • A method to change its x and y coordinates by a given amount and then repaint the object.
  • The panel should use a mouse listener's mousePressed() method to check whether the mouse button is pressed down. mousePressed() should then:
    • Get the position of the mouse event by calling MouseEvent's getX() and getY() methods.
    • Check whether the mouse's x and y coordinates are inside the object. If the mouse position is inside the object, set a moving object variable to mean that the object is moving and save the mouse's x and y coordinates.
      • The BakersDozen program used the moving object itself, set to a value if the object was moving, or set to null if the object was not moving. You could instead use a boolean variable that's true if the object is moving and false if the object is not moving.
  • The panel should use a mouse motion listener's mouseDragged() method to detect when the mouse is moved while the mouse's left button is down. mouseDragged() should then:
    • Get the position of the mouse event by calling MouseEvent's getX() and getY() methods.
    • If the value of the moving object variable means that the object is moving, compare the mouse's new x and y coordinates with the saved x and y coordinates, then move the object the same amount by calling the object's method to change its coordinates.
    • Repaint the panel.
  • The panel should use a mouse listener's mouseReleased() method to detect when the mouse button is released. mouseReleased() should then:
    • Get the position of the mouse event by calling MouseEvent's getX() and getY() methods.
    • If the value of the moving object variable means that the object is moving, set value of the moving object variable to mean it is to not moving.
    • Repaint the panel.
  • The panel's paintComponent() method should call the object's draw method with the panel's Graphics object.

You've now completed the tenth, and last, program in this book! Along the way you've learned about the most common graphics and event-driven programming techniques. Enjoy using this foundation to create more of your own programs!

Appendix A - Glossary

action listener

Action listeners are classes that extend the ActionListener class. They wait for ActionEvents. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons.

ActionEvent

An ActionEvent is an event caused by the program user clicking a button, a radio button, a check box, or a menu item, or by the user selecting an item from a list or pressing enter in a text field. Add an ActionListener to a component to run code when an ActionEvent occurs. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons. See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Event Source. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars.

ActionListener

An ActionListener waits for an ActionEvent from its assigned component. When an ActionEvent occurs, Java calls the ActionListener's actionPerformed() method. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars.

alpha

Colors can be created from four integer values: red, green, blue, and alpha. The alpha value, also known as the alpha channel, sets the transparency of a color. The alpha value can be any value from 0 through 255, where 0 is totally transparent and 255 is totally opaque. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images.

anti-maze

An anti-maze is a maze in which the user may only cross lines. He may not cross open areas. See Lesson 7.3 - Button Focus.

array

An array is one kind of Java list. Array elements may be either Java primitives or Java Objects, but they must all be the same type. The size of the array is set as part of the array declaration and cannot be changed. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.4 - Arrays in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.5 - Empty Array in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

ArrayList

An ArrayList is one kind of Java list. An ArrayList can only hold Java Objects, not Java primitives, and all elements in the list must be of the same type. The size of the ArrayList can be changed at any time by adding or removing elements. See Lesson 15.5 - Array Lists in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

axis

An axis is a straight line going in a particular direction. Locations and directions in a component are referred to in terms of the x-axis (a straight horizontal line, or a row) and the y-axis (a straight vertical line, or column). See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts.

background color

A component is filled with its background color before its text or other details are added in the foreground color. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Panels, Predefined Colors.

block of code

A block of code is a group of zero or more lines of program code, surrounded by curly brackets, { }. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

bold

Bold text is darker and wider than normal, plain text. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.3 - Font.

boolean

Boolean is a basic data type. A boolean variable can have only two possible values, true or false. To use a boolean value in a program, type “true” or “false”, but without the quotes. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.5 - Boolean Data Type in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

BorderLayout

The BorderLayout is a layout best used whenever components should be arranged in these five areas: across the top (PAGE_START), across the bottom (PAGE_END), along the left side between the top and bottom (LINE_START), along the right side between the top and bottom (LINE_END), and in the center (CENTER). Only one component is allowed in each of these areas. The components will be stretched to fill their assigned area. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.1 - Border Layout.

BoxLayout

The BoxLayout is a layout best used whenever any number of components should be arranged in a row (X_AXIS) or in a column (Y_AXIS). The components in a row layout might get stretched vertically and the components in a column layout might get stretched horizontally. See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts.

break

A break statement is used to break out of a switch statement instead of running the next line of code. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Switch Statements in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

BufferedImage

A BufferedImage is a Java object that allows access to image data. For example, individual pixels in the image may be changed. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - New Graphics, Scale an Image. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images.

BufferedReader

A BufferedReader reads character data files more efficiently than FileReaders or InputStreamReaders. Therefore, FileReaders and InputStreamReaders are typically used to create BufferedReaders, and then programs read file data using BufferedReaders. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.2 - Read from a File, Catch Multiple Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File.

BufferedWriter

A BufferedWriter writes to character data files more efficiently than FileWriters. Therefore, FileWriters are typically used to create BufferedWriters, and then programs write file data using the BufferedWriter. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Write to a File in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

build path

The build path is a list of all the other Java projects and code-containing libraries that the current Java project needs to use. See Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Add a Project to the Build Path in Appendix D - Using Eclipse.

button

A button usually refers to a clickable component in a window. When the component is clicked, an ActionEvent is sent. If the program is listening for the event, the program will usually respond in some way. Use the JButton class to create a button or a JRadioButton to create a radio button. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons. See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.1 - A Custom Button, this. See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.2 - In Focus Mark. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.1 - Buttons with Images. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.3 - Button Focus. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.6 - A Default Button. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars.

A button may also refer to one of the buttons on the mouse. For example, the left mouse button would be used for a left-click. See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.3 - Move Objects.

button group

A button group is used to create a set of radio buttons. Only one radio button in the group may be selected at a time. When a radio button in the group is selected, the previously selected radio button will be deselected. Use the ButtonGroup class to create a button group. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons.

ButtonGroup

ButtonGroup is the class used to define a button group. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons.

byte

Byte is a basic data type. A byte variable can hold integers between -128 and 128. To use a byte value in a program, type the value without the quotes. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Integer Data Type and Addition in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

call

When a method is called, the program runs the code in that method before running the code that follows the method call. See Lesson 6.3 - Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

case

A case label marks the code to run for one of the expected values of the variable used in a switch statement. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Switch Statements in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.4 - Switch Default in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.6 - Case without Break in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.1 - Switch Statement with Integers in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

cast

Cast converts an object of one type to another type. A cast operation is indicated by putting a new type in parentheses before the name of a variable defined with a different type. The variable's class must be a superclass of the type to which the object is being cast. If an object can't be cast to the new type, a run time error will occur. See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Event Source.

character

Character is a basic data type, declared in Java with “char”. A character variable can hold only a single character value. To use a character value in a program, type the character surrounded with single quotes. See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.2 - Character Data Type in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

class

A class is a blueprint from which objects are created. A class defines the information the object can hold and what the object can do. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Create a First Program in Appendix D - Using Eclipse.

clickable

This book refers to an object as clickable if clicking the mouse on the displayed representation of the object will result in the program taking an action. See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.1 - A Custom Button, this. See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners

code

Program code is a series of computer instructions that when run in sequence perform a desired task. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

color

Colors are made up of a combination of red, green, and blue hues, and sometimes an alpha value. The hue and alpha values each range from 0 through 255. The higher the hue number, the more of that hue is in the color. Java provides predefined color variables for commonly used colors. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Panels, Predefined Colors. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.6 - Custom Colors. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images.

comment

Comments are notes put in code to explain what the code is intended to do, or to label sections of code. Comments are ignored when the program is run. Comments are lines that begin with // or groups of lines that begin with /* and end with */. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Comments in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

component

A component is any window object that can be added to a Java window. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Add Text, Window Size. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Panels, Predefined Colors. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons. See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.1 - Text Areas. See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.2 - Scroll Bars. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.3 - Add and Remove Components. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.3 - Space Between Components. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars.

component listener

Component listeners are classes that extend the ComponentListener class. They wait for ComponentEvents. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window.

ComponentAdapter

A ComponentAdapter is a class that makes creating a ComponentListener object easier. Using a ComponentAdapter, a programmer writes code only for the ComponentListener's methods that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the defined ComponentListener methods. A ComponentAdapter may be used wherever a ComponentListener is required. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window.

ComponentEvent

A ComponentEvent is an event caused by a component changing size, location, or visibility. Add a ComponentListener or ComponentAdapter to a component to run code when the ComponentEvent occurs. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window.

ComponentListener

A ComponentListener waits for a ComponentEvent from its assigned component. When a ComponentEvent occurs, Java calls the ComponentListener's componentHidden(), componentMoved(), componentResized(), or componentShown() methods. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window.

compress

To compress something is to make it smaller to take less space. Different image formats use different compression techniques to make the image file smaller. Zip files and JAR files contain compressed files to take less space.

confirm dialog

A confirm dialog is a dialog that asks the user a question and waits for an answer. Though a confirm dialog can request other combinations of answers, this book uses confirm dialogs that expect only a yes or no answer. Use JOptionPane to easily create a confirm dialog. See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.4 - Confirm Dialogs.

console

The console displays Java error messages, or the program's System.out messages. In Eclipse, the console is usually displayed in the bottom pane of the window. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - Try/Catch Blocks and Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Print to the Console in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

constructor

A constructor is a special method that is called to create an object of that class. See Key Points and More in Lesson 16.2 - Constructors in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

container

A container is a window component that can hold more than one component, including other containers. JFrame and JPanel are both container components. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Add Text, Window Size. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension.

convert

When a variable's value is converted, some form of calculation is used to create a value of a different type. For example, a string value can be converted to an integer value or a string value can be converted to all upper case letters. Note that the program converts the value from a variable. It does not convert the type of the variable itself. A variable's type is set when it is declared. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - Convert a String to an Integer in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Project 10 - Temperature Converter. See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.4 - Convert a String to Upper Case in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

coordinates

The coordinates of a Java object refer to its x and y location in its container. A location may be the location of the window on the screen, or the location of a component within another component. The x value is the number of pixels to the left edge of the object from the left edge of its container, and the y value is the number of pixels to the top of the object from the top edge of its container. See Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, Lines, Circles, and Preferred Size. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - New Graphics, Scale an Image. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.2 - Draw Strings, Font Metrics.

crop

To crop an image, select a rectangular region of the image to keep. Any part of the image outside of that rectangular area will be removed. See Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars.

Date

The Date class in Java represents a specific instance in time, exact to the nearest millisecond. When a new Date object is created with no parameter values, the Date object's time is set to the time maintained by the computer. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.4 - Current Date, Date Format.

DateFormat

The Java DateFormat class represents many different kinds of date formats. DateFormat has methods that are common to all date formats. However, to work with a date format object, the program must first identify the type of the date format. A SimpleDateFormat is one kind of DateFormat. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.4 - Current Date, Date Format.

declare

When you declare a variable, you state that the variable exists, assign the variable's properties, and optionally assign the variable an initial value. The declaration of a method refers to the statement at the beginning of the method definition that lists the method's properties, return type, name, and parameters. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.3 - Variables, Strings, and the Escape Character in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.3 - Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.3 - Methods that Return a Value in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.3 - Methods with Multiple Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

decrement

To decrement a variable, decrease its value by a small amount, usually 1. See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.3 - Increment Integers in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

default

A default action is taken if no other action was defined. For example, if no layout is defined for a JFrame, Java will use the BorderLayout by default. If no color is defined for a JPanel, it will be gray by default.

default button

The default button means the same as the default enter button. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.6 - A Default Button.

default enter button

The default enter button is the button that will act as though it was clicked when someone presses the enter key, even when another component in the window has focus. For example, a window with input fields and a default enter button allows the program user to type in an input field and press the enter key to activate the default button without using the mouse. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.6 - A Default Button.

define

When you define a class or method, you assign the class or method its properties, and provide code for what the class or method does. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.3 - Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.3 - Methods that Return a Value in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.3 - Methods with Multiple Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

diagonal

A diagonal line is a line that goes up or down the same or opposite amount that the line goes left or right.

dialog

A dialog is a small window that displays a message or gets input from the user. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.8 - Message Dialogs. See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.4 - Confirm Dialogs. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - File Choosers. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.1 - A Custom Dialog. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.3 - Get Dialog Data.

Dimension

A Dimension is a class that holds two integers, usually representing width and height. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension.

disable

If a component is disabled, it will no longer listen for events or allow input. See Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts.

double

Double is a basic data type. A double variable can hold decimal numbers with as many as 16 decimal places. To use a double value in a program, type the number with a decimal point and no quotes. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.6 - Double Data Type in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

element

An element is a data item in an array or ArrayList. Refer to a specific element in an array or ArrayList by giving its index, its position in the array or ArrayList. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.4 - Arrays, Key Points and More in Lesson 14.5 - Empty Array, and Lesson 15.5 - Array Lists in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

ellipsis

An ellipsis is a series of three dots, …, usually used to indicate that some information has been omitted. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.3 - Font.

Ellipses are used in the code listings in this book to represent lines of code that are not shown.

else block

An else block is an optional block of code added to the end of an if statement. The else block runs only if the if statement test evaluates to false. See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

enable

If a component is enabled, it will listen for events and allow input. See Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts.

event

An event is used to indicate that an action was taken on a component, usually by a program user. Examples of events are a mouse clicked, a key pressed, a button clicked, or a window resized. See the Introduction. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons. See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Event Source. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners. See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners.

event queue

Java's event queue is a list used as a control mechanism for handling events from a window's many different inputs. All swing components use the event queue for handling events. Components created in the main() method require code to add the component to the event queue. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.9 - Event Queue.

event-driven programming

Event-driven programming is a style of programming in which the program sets up the desired environment, then just waits for events. The program then responds to the events as they occur, in whatever order they happen. See the Introduction.

exception

An exception occurs when Java doesn't know how to handle a situation that occurs while running code. For example, an exception will occur if the program tries to convert a string with alphabetic characters into an integer, or if the program tries to read from a file that does not exist. The program should include try/catch blocks with code for handling anticipated exception occurrences. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - Try/Catch Blocks and Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

export

Exporting a program takes the program out of Eclipse and puts it in a separate JAR file. The program can then be run without Eclipse by double-clicking on the name of the JAR file. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Export a Program in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Export a Program in Appendix D - Using Eclipse.

extend

A class may already exist that provides functionality close to that needed for a new class. Instead of adding more variables and methods to the first class, and instead of repeating all the first class's variables and methods in the new class, define the new class to extend the first class. The original class then serves as the superclass of the new class. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

extract

Extracting files is the process of copying and decompressing the files that are stored in a ZIP file or JAR file into another folder on the computer. See Download and Install Eclipse in Appendix C - Setup. See Download MoreDIYJava.zip Detailed Instructions in Appendix C - Setup.

File

The Java File class allows programs to work with the contents of a file and its path name. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - File Choosers. See Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts.

file chooser

A file chooser is a dialog that allows the user to browse through a list of files on his computer and choose a file to use in the program. Create a file chooser using JFileChooser. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - File Choosers.

file filter

A file filter applied to a file chooser will restrict the files in the chooser's list by some criteria. For example, a file filter could be added to include only those files with a specific file name extension. Create a file filter using the FileFilter class. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.3 - An Image File Filter.

FileFilter

FileFilter is the class that should be extended to create a file filter. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.3 - An Image File Filter.

FileNotFoundException

A FileNotFoundException is an exception thrown when the program tries to read from a file that does not exist. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.2 - Read from a File, Catch Multiple Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

FileReader

A FileReader reads character data from a file. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.2 - Read from a File, Catch Multiple Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

FileWriter

A FileWriter writes character data to a file. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Write to a File in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

final

The value of a variable declared with the final attribute is set and then never changed by the program. See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.6 - Static Final Variables in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

float

Float is a basic data type in Java. A float variable can hold a decimal number with as many as 7 decimal places. To use a float value in a program, type the value with a decimal point, add an “f” to the end of the value, and use no quotes. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.6 - Double Data Type in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

FlowLayout

The FlowLayout is a layout best used whenever any number of components should be arranged in a row, and each displayed at its preferred size. However, additional rows will be created in a FlowLayout if not all the components fit within the width of the container. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension.

focus

The component in focus will receive keyboard input. Only one component will be in focus at a time. Focus is often referred to as keyboard focus. See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.2 - In Focus Mark. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.3 - Button Focus. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners.

focus listener

Focus listeners are classes that extend the FocusListener class. They wait for FocusEvents. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners.

focus mark

Focus mark refers to the mark that gets painted on a component when the component is in focus. For example, a button will have a rectangle painted around the button's text when the button is in focus. See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.2 - In Focus Mark.

FocusAdapter

A FocusAdapter is a class that makes creating a FocusListener object easier. Using a FocusAdapter, a programmer writes code only for the FocusListener's methods that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the defined FocusListener methods. A FocusAdapter may be used wherever a FocusListener is required. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners.

FocusEvent

A FocusEvent is an event caused by a component coming into focus or going out of focus. Add a FocusListener to a component to run code when the FocusEvent occurs. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners.

FocusListener

A FocusListener waits for a FocusEvent from its assigned component. When a FocusEvent occurs, Java calls the FocusListener's focusGained() or focusLost() method. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners.

font

A font defines how characters will be drawn to the display. A font defines the type design, style, and size of the characters. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.3 - Font. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.2 - Draw Strings, Font Metrics.

font metrics

Font metrics are the measurements of how text is rendered in a specific font. A font metrics object can calculate the measurements of text, or of portions of character symbols. Use FontMetrics to create font metrics. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.2 - Draw Strings, Font Metrics.

FontMetrics

FontMetrics is the class used to create a font metrics object. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.2 - Draw Strings, Font Metrics.

for loop

A for loop is a block of code that repeats a set number of times. A for loop typically initializes an iteration variable, increments or decrements the iteration variable, and terminates when the iteration variable reaches a particular value. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.1 - For Loops in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

foreground color

The foreground color is the color used for the text or symbols that are drawn onto a component. For example, the circle for a radio button will be drawn in the foreground color. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.4 - Foreground Color.

format

Format refers to the way items are arranged or to a pattern. For example, code may be formatted with blocks of code indented, or a date may be formatted using two-digit values for month, day, and year, each separated with a forward slash.

glue component

Glue components are often added to a container with BoxLayout, to add space between other components. Glue components are invisible and will stretch in size equally to use up any extra space in that row or column. To add an exact amount of space that won't stretch, use a rigid component instead. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.3 - Space Between Components. See Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window.

graphical user interface

A graphical user interface, often abbreviated as a GUI, is a visual way for program users to interact with a computer. A GUI consists of a window, plus buttons, menus, and any other visual input methods that allow a user to express what he wants the program to do. See Lesson 2.1 - Border Layout.

graphics

Graphics are usually any sort of visual image or design. See the Introduction.

Graphics

The Graphics class allows a program to draw, scale, or rotate the contents of an image, or to draw on a component. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, Lines, Circles, and Preferred Size. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - New Graphics, Scale an Image. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.2 - Draw Strings, Font Metrics. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.4 - XOR Mode.

GridLayout

The GridLayout is a layout best used whenever components should be arranged in a grid, with each section the same size. If components are not all the same size, they will be stretched so they are displayed the same size. See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.2 - Grid Layout.

GUI

GUI stands for Graphical User Interface. See Lesson 2.1 - Border Layout.

hardware

Hardware is the physical part of a computer: the hard drive, keyboard, mouse, etc. The operating system allows software to interact with the computer hardware.

horizontal alignment

Use a label's setHorizontalAlignment0 method to horizontally align text in a label. Use a container's setAlignmentX() method to horizontally align a component in its container. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.4 - Align Text. See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts

if statement

An if statement is a block of code that runs only if the specified test evaluates to true. An if statement may also have an optional else block that runs only if the test evaluates to false. See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

Image

The Image class represents many different kinds of images. Image provides methods that are common to all images. However, a program must first identify the Image type. A BufferedImage is one kind of Image. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - New Graphics, Scale an Image. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.2 - Save an Image.

image button

An image button is a button that displays an image instead of text. Create an image button using JButton with an ImageIcon. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.1 - Buttons with Images. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars

image label

An image label is a label that displays an image instead of text. Create an image label using JLabel with an ImageIcon. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars.

ImageIcon

ImageIcon is the class for images used in buttons and labels. An ImageIcon object is typically a small image and is easily loaded into the program using the file name or URL. An ImageIcon is not a type of Image, so an ImageIcon may not be used where Images are expected, nor may an Image be used where an ImageIcon is expected. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.1 - Buttons with Images. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.2 - Save an Image.

ImageIO

ImageIO is a class for reading and writing image files of various types. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.2 - Save an Image. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images.

import

Java must have the full, proper name of every class it uses in a program, including the class package name. Import statements give the full name of all non-standard classes used in the program, so that those class names may be used later without their package names. Import a class by adding an import statement for that class at the beginning of the class definition. See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.2 - Generate Random Numbers in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

increment

To increment a variable, increase its value by a small amount, usually 1. See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.3 - Increment Integers in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

index

An index is the position of an item in an ordered collection of items. For example, indexes are used to name the position of a character in a string, or an element in an array. The iteration variable in a for loop is sometimes referred to as the loop index. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.4 - Index of Characters in a String in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.3 - Index of Next Character in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

initialize

To initialize a variable, assign its first value. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.3 - Variables, Strings, and the Escape Character in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

input

Input used as a noun is data that the user enters into a program while the program is running. Input is used as a verb when a user inputs his data into a program. Input is also the name of a method: input(). The text-based programs from Do-It-Yourself Java Games call input() to wait for the user to enter his data. See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.1 - Input a String in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.4 - Check User Input in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

input field

An input field is a component that allows a program user to enter character data to be used by a program. Create an input field using JTextField or JTextArea. See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.1 - Text Areas. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners.

input stream

An input stream reads non-character data from a file. Create an input stream using InputStream. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File.

InputStream

The InputStream class is used to create an input stream of non-character data. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File.

InputStreamReader

The InputStreamReader class is used to read non-character data from an input stream and convert it into character data. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File.

instance

A class is a definition of an object. An object, or class instance, is created from a class definition. See Key Points and More in Lesson 16.1 - Objects, Card in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

instance variable

An instance variable is a variable declared in a class definition instead of in a method. Such a variable may be used by any of the methods defined by that class, without the variable being passed to the methods as a parameter value. See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.3 - Instance Variables in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

int

Int is a basic data type in Java. An int variable can hold an integer value between -2,147,483,648 and 2,147,483,647. To use an int value in a program, type the value without quotes. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Integer Data Type and Addition in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

integer

An integer is a whole number value, either positive or negative. An integer value is typed without quotes or a decimal point. Integer variables are declared in Java as “int”, “byte”, “short”, or “long”. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Integer Data Type and Addition in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - Convert a String to an Integer in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.5 - Integer Subtraction, Multiplication, and Division in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

invalid

If something, for example data provided by a user, is invalid, it is not valid, not allowed. See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.4 - Check User Input in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

IOException

An IOException is an exception thrown when an error occurs as a program tries to read from or write to a file. For example, the IOException is thrown if a file that exists can't be opened. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Write to a File in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.2 - Read from a File, Catch Multiple Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

italic

Italic text is text whose characters are displayed as sloping to the right. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.3 - Font.

iteration variable

An iteration variable is a variable declared in a for loop, incremented or decremented each time through the loop, and compared against another value as a loop exit test. The iteration variable, sometimes also called the loop index or loop control variable, is used to control the number of times the for loop runs. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.1 - For Loops in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

JAR file

A JAR file is a Java Archive file. It contains one or more folders or files of Java program code. A JAR file is named with “.jar” as its extension. If the JAR file is created as a Java executable file, the program in the JAR file can be run by simply double-clicking on the name of the JAR file. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - Java Projects and Packages in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Export a Program in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File.

Java project

The Java Project is the highest level of organization of Java code in Eclipse. Each program in this book is organized in a separate Java project in Eclipse. The Java project contains one or more packages, and each package contains one or more classes. Because the programs are small, most of the Java projects in this book contain only one package. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - Java Projects and Packages in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Create a First Project in Appendix D - Using Eclipse.

JButton

JButton is the class used for creating buttons. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons. See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.1 - A Custom Button, this. See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - Another Custom Button. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.1 - Buttons with Images.

JDialog

JDialog is the class used for creating custom dialogs. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.1 - A Custom Dialog.

JFrame

JFrame is the class used for creating windows. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - A Standard Window. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Add Text, Window Size. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.5 - Pack a Window. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.6 - Disable Resizing. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.7 - Window Title, Center.

JFileChooser

JFileChooser is the class used for creating file choosers. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - File Choosers.

JLabel

JLabel is the class used for creating labels. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Add Text, Window Size. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars.

JMenu

JMenu is the class used for creating menus. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars.

JMenuBar

JMenuBar is the class used for creating a menu bar. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars.

JMenuItem
