JMenuItem is the class used for creating menu items. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars.

JOptionPane

JOptionPane is the class that eases displaying message dialogs or confirm dialogs. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.8 - Message Dialogs. See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.4 - Confirm Dialogs.

JPanel

JPanel is the class used for creating panels. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Panels, Predefined Colors.

JPEG

JPEG is a format for image files. JPEG stands for Joint Photographic Experts Group. A JPEG file is usually named with “.jpg” as its extension. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.2 - Save an Image. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images.

JRadioButton

JRadioButton is the class used for creating radio buttons. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons.

JScrollPane

JScrollPane is the class used for adding scroll bars to any component. See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.2 - Scroll Bars.

JTextArea

JTextArea is the class used for creating large text fields that have multiple rows and columns. JTextAreas are usually used as input fields. See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.1 - Text Areas.

JTextField

JTextField is the class used for creating text input fields. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons.

JToolBar

JToolBar is the class used for creating toolbars. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars.

key code

The key code of a KeyEvent is a number that represents the key on the keyboard that was pressed. Key codes are static integer variables whose name starts with VK_. The key code represents which key was pressed, not the character value of the key. VK stands for virtual key. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners.

key listener

Key listeners are classes that extend the KeyListener class. They wait for KeyEvents. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners.

KeyAdapter

A KeyAdapter is a class that makes creating a KeyListener object easier. Using a KeyAdapter, a programmer writes code only for the KeyListener's methods that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the defined KeyListener methods. A KeyAdapter may be used wherever a KeyListener is required. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners.

keyboard input

Keyboard input refers to data that comes to a program as a results of a user pressing keys on a keyboard. Input fields could be used for keyboard input. Or a key listener could be created to listen for keyboard input. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons.

KeyEvent

A KeyEvent is an event caused by a program user pressing a key on a keyboard. Add a KeyListener to a component to run code when the KeyEvent occurs. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners.

KeyListener

A KeyListener waits for a KeyEvent from its assigned component. When a KeyEvent occurs, Java calls the KeyListener's keyPressed(), keyReleased(), or keyTyped() method. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners.

keystroke

A keystroke is the act of pressing a keyboard key. Programs can process data about a keystroke that includes any modifiers added to the key, such as Alt, Ctrl, Shift, or mouse button down. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners.

label

A label usually consists of a single line of text displayed in a container. However, an image or a combination of both image and text can also serve as a label. Create a label using JLabel. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Add Text, Window Size. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars.

layout

A container's layout defines how components will be arranged in the container. Java calculates the best fit, considering each component's size, the layout chosen, and the system's defined look and feel. Layouts covered in this book include BorderLayout, BoxLayout, FlowLayout, and GridLayout. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.1 - Border Layout. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension. See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.2 - Grid Layout. See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts.

liability

Liability refers to responsibility for what happens. A liability disclaimer is a statement denying responsibility for any potential outcome. See Project 3 - Wizard of Yes/No Disclaimer.

library

Eclipse refers to external JAR files as libraries. For example, DIYJava.jar is a JAR file that must be added as a library in the build path of any Java project that uses the DIYWindow class. See Lesson 1.1 - Java Projects and Packages in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

listen

Program code listens for a user action on a component, waiting for a specific kind of event. Each type of action requires a different listener. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons. See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Event Source. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners. See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners.

listener

A listener is code written to listen for events. Different kinds of events, such as when a program user clicks a mouse button, may be recognized by different listeners, such as a mouse listener. Each type of listener is defined in a separate class, such as a MouseListener. Each class provides different methods for processing an event, such as mousePressed() or mouseReleased(). See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners. See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners.

listing

A program listing usually shows all the program code in a file. The listings in this book are only partial listings, with an ellipsis, …, indicating where code from the file is not shown. See Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Appendix B - Completed Listings.

logical and operator

The logical and operator, &&, is used to determine whether two tests both evaluate to true. If the test on the left side is false, Java does not perform the test on the right side. See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

logical or operator

The logical or operator, ||, is used to determine whether at least one of two tests evaluates to true. If the test on the left side is true, Java does not perform the test on the right side. See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

long

A long is a basic data type in Java. A long variable can hold an integer value between -9,223,372,036,854,775,808 and 9,223,372,036,854,775,807. To use a long value in a program, type the value without quotes. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Integer Data Type and Addition in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

look and feel

The look and feel of a system refers to how the operating system displays components and how the components work on the operating system. Windows, OS X, and Linux components all look and behave differently. A Java programmer can set the look and feel for a program, independent of the operating system used to run that program. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.10 - Cross Platform Look and Feel.

main() method

The main() method is the first method called when a program starts. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

maximized

When a window is maximized, it fills the entire display area of the computer's monitor or screen. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position.

menu

A menu is a drop down list of one or more choices, called menu items, on a menu bar. Use a JMenu to create a menu. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars.

menu bar

A menu bar is a row of one or more menus, usually stretched across the top of a container. Use a JMenuBar to create a menu bar. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars.

menu item

A menu item is a clickable choice in a menu. When the menu item is clicked, an ActionEvent is sent. If the program is listening for the event, the program will usually respond in some way. Use a JMenuItem to create a menu item. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars.



message dialog

A message dialog is a dialog whose purpose is simply to display a message. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.8 - Message Dialogs.

method

A method is a named block of code that can be called from within the program. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.3 - Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.3 - Methods that Return a Value in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.3 - Methods with Multiple Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

millisecond

A millisecond is 1/1000 of a second.

minimized

When a window is minimized, it is removed from the screen but the program that displayed it is still running and accessible. In Microsoft Windows, a minimized window is displayed as an icon in the task bar. Clicking on the window's icon in the task bar will return the window to the display, at the window's previous size. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position.

modal

A dialog may be modal or non-modal. When a modal dialog is displayed, the program stops to wait for the user to close the dialog. Use a modal dialog if the program should wait for user input before proceeding. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.3 - Get Dialog Data.

monospaced font

In a monospaced font, all the characters have the same width. In contrast, each character in a proportional font may have a different width. For example, in a monospaced font, such as Courier New, the letters “i” and “W” have the same width. In a proportional font, such as Times New Roman”, the letter “W” is much wider than the letter “i”. See Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

mouse listener

Mouse listeners are classes that extend the MouseListener class. They wait for MouseEvents. See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners.

mouse motion listener

Mouse motion listeners are classes that extend the MouseMotionListener class. They wait for MouseEvents. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners.

MouseAdapter

A MouseAdapter is a class that makes creating a MouseListener object easier. Using a MouseAdapter, a programmer writes code only for the MouseListener's methods that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the defined MouseListener methods. A MouseAdapter may be used wherever a MouseListener is required. See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners.

MouseEvent

A MouseEvent is an event caused by a program user clicking a mouse button. Add a MouseListener or a MouseMotionListener to a component to run code when a MouseEvent occurs. See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners.

MouseListener

A MouseListener waits for a MouseEvent from its assigned component. When a MouseEvent occurs, Java calls the MouseListener's mouseClicked(), mouseEntered(), mouseExited(), mousePressed(), or mouseReleased() method. See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners.

MouseMotionAdapter

A MouseMotionAdapter is a class that makes creating a MouseMotionListener object easier. Using a MouseMotionAdapter, a programmer writes code only for the MouseMotionListener's methods that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the defined MouseMotionListener methods. A MouseMotionAdapter may be used wherever a MouseMotionListener is required. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners.

MouseMotionListener

A MouseMotionListener waits for a MouseEvent from its assigned component. When a MouseEvent occurs, Java calls the MouseMotionListener's mouseDragged() or mouseMoved() method. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners.

non-modal

A dialog may be modal or non-modal. When a non-modal dialog is displayed, the program continues to run. Use a non-modal dialog if the program user should continue interacting with the rest of the program while the dialog is displayed. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.3 - Get Dialog Data.

not operator

The not operator, !, inverts the value of a boolean or returns the complement of a test evaluation. For example, !true returns false. See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

null

null means on object has no value, not even a blank or a 0. A program will receive an error if it tries to use a variable whose value is null for anything other than to check its value. To use a null value in a program, type “null”, but without the quotes.

NumberFormatException

A NumberFormatException is an exception thrown if a program cannot successfully convert a value to a number. For example, if a program tries to convert “abc” to a number, that program will throw a NumberFormatException. See Lesson 8.4 - Try/Catch Blocks and Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

object

An object is an instance of a class. The object holds the information defined in the class and can be operated on by the class's methods. See Key Points and More in Lesson 16.1 - Objects, Card in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

A Java class named Object is the base class of all Java classes. See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Event Source.

opaque

Opaque entities are solid. A user cannot see through an opaque object. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.5 - Opacity.

operating system

The operating system is the software on the computer that manages how other programs interact with each other and with the hardware of the computer. Examples of operating systems include Windows, OS X, or Linux. See Appendix C - Setup.

override

Consider overriding a method whenever the class's superclass has a method that you would like to behave differently. To override a method, create a second method, with the exact same name, static modifier, return type, and parameters as the first method. The second method's visibility doesn't have to be identical, but the second method cannot be more visible than the method being overridden. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners.

pack

Packing a window tells Java to resize the window and arrange all of its components in the smallest possible area, considering all the components' layouts and preferred sizes. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.5 - Pack a Window.

package

Packages contain one or more class files that are typically used together. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - Java Projects and Packages in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Create a First Package in Appendix D - Using Eclipse.

panel

A panel is a container that can hold many components, including other panels. Use JPanel to create panels. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Panels, Predefined Colors. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension.

Panels are also often used as drawing surfaces for program-created objects for which Java has no components, such as dice, letter tiles, and cards. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, lines, Circles, and Preferred Size.

parameter

Methods are defined to expect zero or more input values. These expected input values are declared in the method as parameters, each with a variable type and name. The method then uses those variables to access the parameter values passed to the method when the method is called. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.3 - Methods with Multiple Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

parameter value

A parameter value is passed into a method that has defined parameters, when the method is called. The method may then use that value in its code. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.3 - Methods with Multiple Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

pass

Passing a value to a method with defined parameters means the program sends the value to the method as a parameter value, when the method is called. See Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

pixel

The term pixel originated from the phrase “picture element”. A pixel is the smallest possible element of a picture. In Java, pixel refers to the smallest point defined for an image or the screen. For example, an image whose resolution is 640 by 480 is made up of 640 rows and 480 columns of pixels.

PNG

PNG is a format for image files. “PNG” stands for Portable Network Graphics. A PNG file is usually named with “.png” as its extension. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images.

Point

A Point is a class that holds two integers, usually representing x and y coordinates. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position.

preferred size

The preferred size of a component consists of the preferred width and height values (a Dimension) the programmer desired for the component. Some layouts display components at their preferred size, others do not. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension.

Always provide the preferred size of a panel that holds no components, such as a panel used as a drawing surface, by overriding the panel's getPreferredSize() method. Otherwise, no space may be reserved for that panel in the layout. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, Lines, Circles, and Preferred Size.

primitive

The Java primitive data types are int, double, char, boolean, byte, short, long, and float. The primitive types require no class definitions, and are manipulated using language-defined operations, rather than by calling a methods. See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.5 - Array Lists in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

private

A variable or method may be declared as private. A private declaration means that only objects of the class that declared the variable or method can see or use the variable or method. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.3 - Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.3 - Instance Variables in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

programmer

A programmer is a person who writes computer program code.

protected

A variable or method may be declared as protected. A protected declaration means that only objects of the class that declared the variable or method, or objects of any class that extends that class, can see or use the variable or method. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

public

A variable or method may be declared as public. A public declaration means an object of any class in the same build path may see or use the variable or method. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.3 - Instance Variables in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

Quick Fix

The Quick Fix feature of Eclipse lists ways Eclipse thinks a syntax error could be fixed. To use Quick Fix, rest your mouse on the underlined error in the code. Eclipse will list ways to fix the problem. Select one of the options and Eclipse will fix the error for you. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

radio button

A radio button is a clickable component with text. A radio button has only two states: selected or not selected. Use JRadioButton to create radio buttons. Radio buttons are usually added to a button group, in which only one radio button may be selected at a time. Use ButtonGroup to create button groups. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons.

random

If an item in a set is chosen at random, choosing any item is equally likely. See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.2 - Generate Random Numbers in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

ratio

A ratio is a number representing how large one number is compared to the other. For example, if a number is half the size of another number, the numbers have a 1 to 2 ratio. The ratio may be represented as a single number by dividing the two numbers. In other words, the same ratio could be represented as 1/2 or .5. See Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners.

repaint

When a program repaints a component, the program asks Java to draw the entire component again. A component should be repainted whenever the program changes instance variable values that might affect how the component should look. Use the component's repaint() method to repaint the component. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, Lines, Circles, and Preferred Size.

reset

Resetting a variable returns it to its original value.

resize

To resize a component or an image, change its size to a new size. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - New Graphics, Scale an Image. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window. See Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners.

resolved

Getting an error that a variable name cannot be resolved means that Java doesn't know how the variable is defined. This error is usually fixed by declaring the variable before the variable is used. See Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games

Getting an error that a class name cannot be resolved means that Java doesn't know how the class is defined. This error is usually fixed by using Quick Fix to import the needed class.. See Lesson 9.2 - Generate Random Numbers in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

resource

A program's resources include any additional files that are needed for the program to run. The resources often include data files and image files. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars.

respectively

The word “respectively” is often used in this book when referring to a list of variables and a list of their initial values. To set the variables to their values, respectively, means to assign the first value to the first variable, the second value to the second variable, etc.

return

A method may optionally return a value. If a method returns a value, the code that called the method may assign the results of that call to a variable of the same type as the returned value. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.3 - Methods that Return a Value in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

revalidate

When a program revalidates a component, the program is asking Java to again perform the layout of the component, and any components the component contains. A program should revalidate a component when the program adds, removes, or resizes a component or components within that component. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.3 - Add and Remove Components. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, Lines, Circles, and Preferred Size.

rigid component

Rigid components are often added to a BoxLayout to add space between components. Rigid components are invisible, but will take up the exact amount of space defined for them. If a program needs an invisible component that should stretch to fill remaining space, use a glue component instead. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.3 - Space Between Components.

root pane

The JFrame window is actually made up of several panes, one of which is the root pane. Explanation of all these panes is beyond the scope of this book. However, you need to know that if a button should be used as a default button, the program must get the JFrame object's root pane, and set its default button. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.6 - A Default Button.

run

When a program is run, Java calls the program's main() method and runs the instructions of each line of code in sequence. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

run time error

A run time error occurs only when the program is running.

scale

To scale an image, change its size to a new size, usually while keeping the same width to height ratio. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - New Graphics, Scale an Image. See Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners.

scramble

To scramble a group of items, rearrange them in a random order. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Comments in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

scroll bars

Scroll bars are slider components that are added to the side and bottom of a component if the component does not fit in its container. The sliders allow the program user to scroll through the parts of the component that did not fit in the display. Put a component in a JScrollPane to easily add scroll bars to the component. See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.2 - Scroll Bars.

serial version UID

The serial version UID is meant to be a unique ID assigned to the current version of the class. The serial version UID is only used if the class is serialized. None of the classes in this book will be serialized, and serialization is beyond the scope of this book. You may ignore the warning Eclipse gives about the missing serialVersionUID. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.8 - Serial Version UID

short

Short is a basic data type in Java. A short variable can hold an integer value between -32,768 and 32,767. To use a short value in a program, type the value without quotes. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Integer Data Type and Addition in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

SimpleDateFormat

SimpleDateFormat is a class that defines how a Date is to be displayed as a string. For example, a SimpleDateFormat may include month names or month numbers, it may include the time or only the day, and it may include extra characters: comma, slash, dash, colon, or others. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.4 - Current Date, Date Format.

software

Software is another name for a computer program. Software is created from program code written by programmers.

source

Many of the different events have a method to get the source of the event. Getting the source will return the component on which the event occurred. See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Event Source.

statement

A statement is a complete line of code, usually up to and including the ending semicolon. Some statements, such as if statements and switch statements, include a block of code. Such statements end after the block of code instead of after a semicolon. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Switch Statements in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - While Loops in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.1 - For Loops in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

static

Static methods are self-contained. They can only use their parameter values; they cannot use the class's instance variables. A static method may be called by using its class name followed by the method name. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

Static variables are shared by every object created from the class. If one object updates the value of a static variable, all objects created from that class see the same new value for that variable. See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.6 - Static Final Variables in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

string

A string is text with zero or more characters of any kind. String variables are declared in Java as “String”. To use a string value in a program, type the text surrounded with double quotes. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.3 - Variables, Strings, and the Escape Character in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - Convert a String to an Integer in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.1 - Order of Operation in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.2 - String Length and Substring in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.4 - Index of Characters in a String in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.2 - Replace Characters in a String in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

stub

Stub code is an automatically-generated method declaration. The content of the method is left empty for the programmer to write himself. See Create a First Program in Appendix D - Using Eclipse.

subimage

A subimage is a rectangular portion of an image. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons.

superclass

A superclass is a class from which the current class is derived. All classes without a defined superclass have Object as their superclass. Any class may be used as a superclass. An object created from a class is considered to be “a kind of” its superclass, and may use any of the public or protected variables or methods of its superclass. For example, a class which names DIYWindow as its superclass is a kind of DIYWindow and may use the print() and input() methods defined by DIYWindow. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Create a First Program in Appendix D - Using Eclipse.

switch statement

A switch statement is a block of code that runs different code for each expected value of a variable. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Switch Statements in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.4 - Switch Default in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.6 - Case without Break in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.1 - Switch Statement with Integers in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

syntax error

A syntax error occurs if program code does not meet the order or content rules required by Java. All syntax errors must be fixed before a program can run. Eclipse provides a Quick Fix tool to easily fix syntax errors. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

task bar

Microsoft Windows has a task bar, usually displayed across the bottom of the window, that contains an icon for each program that currently displays a window. Clicking any of the icons In the task bar brings that window to the front of the other windows. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.7 - Window Title, Center.

terminate

Terminating a program stops it. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.3 - Infinite Loops in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

text field

A text field is a component that allows the program user to enter one line of character data to be used by the program. Create a text field using JTextField. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners.

throw an exception

When a running program encounters an exception, the program skips to the code that catches that particular exception. If no catch block was written for that exception, the program terminates. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - Try/Catch Blocks and Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

title

A program title is displayed in the title bar of a window or with a program icon in the task bar. Set the title of a program using JFrame's setTitle() method. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.7 - Window Title, Center.

toggle

Toggling causes something to alternate between two possible states, such as between on and off, or between black and white.

toolbar

A toolbar is a row of components, typically stretched across the top of a window. Components in a toolbar are most often added as image buttons, but may also include any other types of components. Each component in a toolbar should have a listener added to it to perform an action when an event occurs on that component. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars

tool tip

Because toolbar components are often images instead of text, the corresponding tool's purpose might not always be obvious. Help the program user understand the tool's purpose by displaying a tool tip. A tool tip is the text displayed when the user rests his cursor on a tool in the toolbar. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars.

transparent

If something is transparent, it is invisible. Users can see through transparent objects. See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.5 - Opacity. See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images.

try/catch block

A try/catch block consists of a try block and one or more catch blocks. Place code that might throw an exception within a try block. Place catch blocks for each expected exception at the end of the try block. Put code inside each catch block to run when that exception is caught. The program will then continue with the code that follows the entire try/catch block. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - Try/Catch Blocks and Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

type

In Java, the type of an object is defined by its class or its superclass. For example, the HelloWorld class created in the first book is a type of DIYWindow; or a variable declared as a String has String as its type. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

unhandled exception

An unhandled exception is an exception for which no handling code is provided. Add a try/catch block to handle exceptions. A program will stop with a run time error if the program runs into an unhandled exception. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - Try/Catch Blocks and Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

unicode

Unicode provides a common representation of text characters that is meant to be independent of the device, program, or language that is working with the text. Unicode numbers have been assigned for all of the typable characters as well as for many symbols not found on a keyboard, such as hearts, diamonds, clubs, and spades. See Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images.

unzip

Unzip is the process of extracting files from a ZIP file. See Download and Install Eclipse in Appendix C - Setup.

user

The user is the person who is running a program. See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.1 - Input a String in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

valid

If something, for example data provided by a user, is valid, it is allowed. See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.4 - Check User Input in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

variable

A variable is a named piece of data whose value can be changed. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.3 - Variables, Strings, and the Escape Character in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.1 - Reuse Strings in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

visible

If a variable or method is visible, it can be seen by other program code. The three different visibility settings are private, protected, and public. See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.3 - Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.3 - Instance Variables in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

A window or dialog must be made visible for it to be displayed. To make a window or dialog visible or invisible, use JFrame's or JDialog's setVisible() method. Instead of closing a dialog after the user enters input, make the dialog not visible so the program can still access the data that the user entered. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - A Standard Window. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.1 - A Custom Dialog. See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.3 - Get Dialog Data.

while loop

A while loop is a block of code that repeats while an expression evaluates to true. See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - While Loops in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

whole number

A whole number is a numeric value with no fractional or decimal part. Whole number variables, more commonly referred to as integers, are declared in Java as “byte”, “short”, “int” or “long”. See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Integer Data Type and Addition in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.

window

A basic window consists of a large rectangular area with a title bar, usually displayed across the top, and a border around the edges. Many other components can be added to a window. Use Java's JFrame class to create a window. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - A Standard Window.

window listener

Window listeners are classes that extend the WindowListener class. They wait for WindowEvents. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position.

window state listener

Window state listeners are classes that extend the WindowStateListener class. They wait for WindowEvents. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window.

WindowAdapter

WindowAdapter is a class that makes creating a WindowListener object easier. Using a WindowAdapter, a programmer must write code only for the WindowListener's methods that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the defined WindowListener methods. A WindowAdapter may be used wherever a WindowListener is required. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position.

WindowEvent

A WindowEvent is an event caused by a window being: opened, closed, newly made active, made no longer active, minimized, or returned to normal size. Add a WindowListener or a WindowStateListener to a component to run code when the WindowEvent occurs. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position.

WindowListener

A WindowListener waits for a WindowEvent from its assigned component. When a WindowEvent occurs, Java calls the WindowListener's windowActivated(), windowClosed(), windowClosing(), windowDeactivated(), windowDeiconified(), windowIconified(), or windowOpened() method. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position.

WindowStateListener

A WindowStateListener waits for a WindowEvent from its assigned component. When a WindowEvent occurs, Java calls the WindowStateListener's windowStateChanged() method. See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window.

word wrap

If word wrap is turned on, words that are too long to fit at the end of a line are moved to the beginning of the next line. See Lesson 1.1 - A Standard Window. See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.1 - Text Areas.

work folder

Create a work folder to contain all the Java code and other files needed for your programs. See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - Java Projects and Packages in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Create a Java Work Folder in Appendix C - Install Required Software and Files in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Create a Java Work Folder in Appendix C - Setup.

x-axis

The x-axis is a straight horizontal line, or a row. See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts.

y-axis

The y-axis is a straight vertical line, or a column. See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts.

ZIP file

A ZIP file contains one or more folders or files. A ZIP file is named with “.zip” as its extension. Files must be extracted from a ZIP file before they can be used. See Download and Install Eclipse in Setup in Do-It-Yourself Java Games. See Download and Install Eclipse in Appendix C - Setup.

  private void scramble() {
    int openRow = gridSize-1;
    int openCol = gridSize-1;
    
    Random rand = new Random();
    
    for (int i=0; i<25*gridSize; i++) {
      int direction = rand.nextInt(gridSize);
      switch(direction) {
      case UP:
        if (openRow > 0) {
          tile[openRow][openCol].swap(tile[openRow-1][openCol]);
          openRow--;
        }
        break;
      case DOWN:
        if (openRow < gridSize-1) {
          tile[openRow][openCol].swap(tile[openRow+1][openCol]);
          openRow++;
        }
        break;
      case LEFT:
        if (openCol > 0) {
          tile[openRow][openCol].swap(tile[openRow][openCol-1]);
          openCol--;
        }
        break;
      case RIGHT:
        if (openCol < gridSize-1) {
          tile[openRow][openCol].swap(tile[openRow][openCol+1]);
          openCol++;
        }
      }
    }    
  }

  private void moveBall(int direction) {
    switch (direction) {
    case KeyEvent.VK_UP :
      // move up if this cell does not have a top wall
      if (!cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.TOP)) {
        moveTo(row-1, col);
      }
      break;
    case KeyEvent.VK_DOWN :
      // move down if this cell does not have a bottom wall
      if (!cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.BOTTOM)) {
        moveTo(row+1, col);
      }
      break;
    case KeyEvent.VK_LEFT :
      // move left if this cell does not have a left wall
      if (!cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.LEFT)) {
        moveTo(row, col-1);
      }
      break;
    case KeyEvent.VK_RIGHT :
      // move right if this cell does not have a right wall
      if (!cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.RIGHT)) {
        moveTo(row, col+1);
      }
      break;
    }
  }

    switch (direction) {
    case UP :
      // move up if this cell does not have a top wall
      if (!cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.TOP)) {
        moveTo(row-1, col, Cell.TOP, Cell.BOTTOM);
      }
      break;
    case DOWN :
      // move down if this cell does not have a bottom wall
      if (!cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.BOTTOM)) {
        moveTo(row+1, col, Cell.BOTTOM, Cell.TOP);
      }
      break;
    case LEFT :
      // move left if this cell does not have a left wall
      if (!cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.LEFT)) {
        moveTo(row, col-1, Cell.LEFT, Cell.RIGHT);
      }
      break;
    case RIGHT :
      // move right if this cell does not have a right wall
      if (!cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.RIGHT)) {
        moveTo(row, col+1, Cell.RIGHT, Cell.LEFT);
      }
      break;
    }

    ...
 
  private void moveBall(int direction) {
    switch (direction) {
    case UP :
      // move up if this cell does not have a top wall
      if (!cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.TOP)) {
        moveTo(row-1, col, Cell.TOP, Cell.BOTTOM);
        // move up more if this is a long column
        while (!cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.TOP)
            && cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.LEFT)
            && cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.RIGHT)) {
          moveTo(row-1, col, Cell.TOP, Cell.BOTTOM);
        }
      }
      break;
    case DOWN :
      // move down if this cell does not have a bottom wall
      if (!cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.BOTTOM)) {
        moveTo(row+1, col, Cell.BOTTOM, Cell.TOP);
        // move down more if this is a long column
        while (!cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.BOTTOM)
            && cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.LEFT)
            && cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.RIGHT)) {
          moveTo(row+1, col, Cell.BOTTOM, Cell.TOP);
        }
      }
      break;
    case LEFT :
      // move left if this cell does not have a left wall
      if (!cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.LEFT)) {
        moveTo(row, col-1, Cell.LEFT, Cell.RIGHT);
        // move left more if this is a long row
        while (!cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.LEFT)
            && cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.TOP)
            && cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.BOTTOM)) {
          moveTo(row, col-1, Cell.LEFT, Cell.RIGHT);
        }
      }
      break;
    case RIGHT :
      // move right if this cell does not have a right wall
      if (!cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.RIGHT)) {
        moveTo(row, col+1, Cell.RIGHT, Cell.LEFT);
        // move right more if this is a long row
        while (!cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.RIGHT)
            && cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.TOP)
            && cell[row][col].isWall(Cell.BOTTOM)) {
          moveTo(row, col+1, Cell.RIGHT, Cell.LEFT);
        }
      }
      break;
    }
  }

        totalCount++;
      }
    }

  private void rollRemainingDice() {
    int count = 0;
    for(int i=0; i<6; i++) {
      if(dice[i].isSelected()) {
        dice[i].hold();
      }
      else if(!dice[i].isHeld()) {
        dice[i].roll();
        count++;
      }
    }
    
    if (count==0) {
      rollAllDice();
    }
  }

    }
    points = 0;
    newPoints = 0;
    pointsLabel.setText("0");

  private void endRound() {
 
      ...
 
    if (round < 10) {
      round++;
      roundLabel.setText("" + round);
      rollAllDice();
    }
    else {
      String message = "Do you want to play again?";
      int option = JOptionPane.showConfirmDialog(this, message, "Play Again?", JOptionPane.YES_NO_OPTION);
      if (option == JOptionPane.YES_OPTION) {
        score = 0;
        round = 1;
        scoreLabel.setText("0");
        roundLabel.setText("1");
        rollAllDice();
      }
      else {
        System.exit(0);
      }
    }
  }

  private void getPreviousHighScore() {
    try {
      BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(new File(FILENAME)));
      String s = in.readLine();
      highScore = Integer.parseInt(s);
      in.close();
    }
    catch (FileNotFoundException e) {
      JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(this, FILENAME + " was not found.");
    }
    catch(IOException e) {
      JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(this, FILENAME + " could not be opened.");
    }
    catch(NumberFormatException e) {
      JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(this, FILENAME + " contains invalid data.");

  public Dictionary() {
    for(int i=0; i<26; i++) {
      wordList[i] = new ArrayList<String>();
    }
    
    BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(FILENAME));
    String word = in.readLine();
    while (word != null) {
      char letter = word.charAt(0);
      int list = ALPHABET.indexOf(letter);
      wordList[list].add(word);
      word = in.readLine();
    }
    in.close();
  }

  public BagOfLetters() {
    for (int i = 0; i<letters.length(); i++) {
      char letter = letters.charAt(i);
      for (int count = 0; count<quantity[i]; count++) {
        LetterPanel letterPanel = new LetterPanel(""+letter, points[i]);
        letterPanels.add(letterPanel);

  public LetterPanel pickALetter() {
    LetterPanel letterPanel = null;
    int size = letterPanels.size();
    if (size>0) {
      int pick = rand.nextInt(size);
      letterPanel = letterPanels.remove(pick);
    }
    return letterPanel;
  }

  private void endGame() {
    ArrayList<String> records = new ArrayList<String>();
    
    try {
      BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(new File(FILENAME)));
      String s = in.readLine();
      while (s!=null) {
        records.add(s);
        s = in.readLine();
      }
      in.close();
    }
    catch(FileNotFoundException e) {
      String message = "File " + FILENAME + " was not found.";
      JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(this, message);
    }
    catch(IOException e) {

    ...
 
  private void endGame() {
    ArrayList<String> records = new ArrayList<String>();
    int index = 0;
    
    try {
      BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(new File(FILENAME)));
      String s = in.readLine();
      while (s!=null) {
        records.add(s);
        int indexOfBlank = s.indexOf(" ");
        String scoreString = s.substring(0, indexOfBlank);
        int oldScore = Integer.parseInt(scoreString);
        if (oldScore>score) {
          index++;
        }
        s = in.readLine();
      }
      in.close();
    }
    catch(FileNotFoundException e) {
      String message = "File " + FILENAME + " was not found.";
      JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(this, message);
    }
    catch(IOException e) {
      String message = "File " + FILENAME + " was could not be opened.";
      JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(this, message);
    }
    catch(NumberFormatException e) {
      String message = "File " + FILENAME + " contains invalid data.\nA new high score list will be created.";
      JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(this, message);
    }
  }

      }

    score = 0;
    points = 0;
    word = "";
    scoreLabel.setText("0");
    updateButtonsAndPoints();
  }

      imagePanel.setImage(newImage);

    ...
 
  private void cropDragged(int x, int y) {
    if (x>startX) {
      cropW = x - startX;
    }
    else {
      cropW = startX - x;
      cropX = x;
    }
    if (y>startY) {
      cropH = y - startY;
    }
    else {
      cropH = startY - y;
      cropY = y;
    }
    imageResizer.setCropFields(cropX, cropY, cropW, cropH);
    repaint();
  }

  public Deck() {
    try {
      InputStream input = getClass().getResourceAsStream(FILENAME);
      BufferedImage cardsImage = ImageIO.read(input);
      for(int suit = 0; suit<SUITSYMBOLS.length; suit++) {
        for(int rank = 0; rank<RANKS.length; rank++) {
          int x = rank*CARDWIDTH;
          int y = suit*CARDHEIGHT;
          Image image = cardsImage.getSubimage(x, y, CARDWIDTH, CARDHEIGHT);
          Card card = new Card(RANKS[rank], suit, VALUES[rank], image);
          cards.add(card);
        }
      }
    }
    catch(IOException e) {
      String message = "Could not open image file " + FILENAME;
      JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(null, message);
    }
  }

  private void released(int x, int y) {
    if (movingCard!=null) {

      // play on a foundation?
      for (int i=0; i<4 && !validMove; i++) {
        int foundationx = foundation[i].getX();
        int foundationy = foundation[i].getY();
        if (movingCard.isNear(foundationx, foundationy)) {
 
          // empty foundation?
          if (foundation[i].size() == 0) {

              validMove = true;
              foundation[i].add(movingCard);
              movingCard = null;

Appendix C - Setup

These installation and setup instructions are designed for Microsoft Windows. The programs that you'll download, install, and create could run on any computer that runs with a Windows, OS X, or Linux operating system. However, this book doesn't describe how to install or set up the programming environment for those other systems.

Create a Java Work Folder

You must create your own Java work folder on your computer. I recommend that you put your Java work folder in your Windows user folder, but you can put your work folder anywhere on your computer. I called mine java and put it in my user folder, c:\Users\Annette. Therefore, my Java work folder is c:\Users\Annette\java.

To create a folder in Windows 7, first click Start / Computer to open Windows Explorer. To create a folder in Windows 10, first click Start / File Explorer. Then click on the name of the folder in which you want to create the new folder, and click the New folder button. Enter a name for your new folder.

If you share your computer with someone else who also wants to program in Java, create a different Java work folder for each of you. Your Java work folders must either have different names, or be in different folders.

  1. Create a Java work folder on your computer now.

Download and Install Java

You'll be writing your computer programs in the Java programming language. Your computer needs the free Java Development Kit to generate programs from Java program code.

The Java Development Kit only needs to be installed one time on your computer, no matter how many people plan to write Java programs on your computer.

To install the Java Development Kit:

  1. Go to http://www.oracle.com/technetwork/java/javase/downloads/index.html.
  2. Click the download button, pictured below, to download the latest version of the Java Development Kit (JDK) for Java Standard Edition (SE)

  1. Accept the license agreement, as shown in the image below. Download either the Windows x86 or Windows x64 version of the Java Development Kit, depending on which version of Windows you have. Windows x86 is for 32-bit Windows; Windows x64 is for 64-bit Windows.
    1. How do you check whether you have 32-bit or 64-bit Windows? In Windows 7, click Start / Control Panel and double-click on System. In Windows 10, click Start / Settings / System / About. The System Type states whether you have the 32-bit or 64-bit operating system. If your Control Panel doesn't have a System icon, you might have to click the View by drop down list in the top right corner of the Control Panel and choose Small Icons.

  1. Double-click the downloaded .exe file name to install Java. You should be able to take all the installation defaults.

Download and Install Eclipse

Eclipse is a free Java development environment. Eclipse makes typing program code easier, identifies programming errors, and even suggests ways to fix those errors.

I recommend that you install Eclipse in your Windows user folder, but you can put Eclipse anywhere on your computer. I put mine in my user folder, c:\Users\Annette.

  1. Download the latest version of Eclipse IDE for Java Developers from http://www.eclipse.org/downloads/. Download either the 32-bit or 64-bit version, depending on which version of Windows you have, to any location on your computer.
  2. To unzip the downloaded .zip file, right-click on its name, choose Extract all..., and browse to the folder into which you want to install Eclipse. I extracted mine into my user folder, c:/Users/Annette.
    1. If you share your computer with someone else who also wants to write Java programs, extract each person's copy of Eclipse into a different folder.

Create a shortcut on your desktop for Eclipse. These instructions are for Windows 7 and 10:

  1. Open the eclipse folder that was created when you extracted the files from the downloaded .zip file. My eclipse folder is in c:/Users/Annette.
  2. Right-click on eclipse.exe and choose copy.
  3. Right-click on your desktop and choose Paste shortcut.
  4. If you aren't the only one who will use Eclipse for programming on your computer, right-click on the shortcut you just created and rename the shortcut for your use. For example, I might rename mine to Eclipse for Annette.
  5. Repeat steps 1-4 for each person who will use Eclipse on your computer, copying the eclipse.exe file that was extracted for them.

Download MoreDIYJava.zip Detailed Instructions

The lessons require a few additional data files. Those files are included in a free .zip file on the Godtland Software website:

  1. Download MoreDIYJava.zip from http://www.godtlandsoftware.com/DIYJava/.
  2. To unzip MoreDIYJava.zip, right-click on MoreDIYJava.zip and choose Extract all.... Use the Browse button to extract the files into your Java work folder. I extracted mine into c:/Users/Annette/java.

Appendix D - Using Eclipse

Set up Eclipse.

  1. Double-click your Eclipse shortcut. This window should appear:

  1. Click the Browse... button to find your Java work folder, as shown in the above screenshot, and then click OK. This window should appear:

  1. Click Workbench to open the main Eclipse window.

Use the Java perspective:

  1. Click Window / Perspective / Open Perspective / Java.

Make more room for writing code:

  1. Close the Task list, as shown in this image:

  1. Move the Outline tab to the bottom of the Package Explorer pane, as shown in this image:

You now have everything you need to create your first program!

Create a First Project

Create your first Java project, called Hello World:

  1. If Eclipse is no longer open:
    1. Double-click the Eclipse shortcut you created on your desktop.
    2. Click OK to use your Java work folder as your workspace.
  2. Right-click in the Package Explorer pane and choose New / Java Project.
  3. Name the Java project Hello World, and select Use Default JRE if it is 1.7 or higher, then click Next as shown below. If the default JRE is less than 1.7, select the option to Use an execution environment JRE of 1.7 or higher.

  1. Click Finish.

The Package Explorer pane should now list the project, Hello World.

Key Points and More

  • Each program in this book will be created in a separate Java project.
  • Program code that will be shared between different programs will be created in a separate Java project as well.
  • Right-click in the Package Explorer pane to create a Java project.
  • Eclipse will create a folder on your computer named the same as the Java project. Give your Java project a name you want to use for the folder on your computer.
    • You now have a folder called Hello World in your Java work folder.
    • For example, capitalize the first letter of each word and put a space between each word like the Hello World project.
  • The minimum JRE requirement for the programs in this book is Java SE 1.7. When you create the Java Projects in this book, make sure you select the option to Use an execution environment JRE of JavaSE-1.7 or higher. Once you select this option for creating a project, Eclipse will default to that option for all Java Projects you create in the future.

Create a First Package

Create a package for your Hello World program in the Hello World project:

  1. Right-click on the Hello World project in the Package Explorer pane and choose New / Package.
  2. Name the package ____________.____________.helloworld, as shown in the image below. Use your own name as part of the package name. I used annette.godtland.helloworld for my package name.

  1. Click Finish.

The Package Explorer pane now shows the package you created in your Hello World project.

Key Points and More

  • Organize your program files into packages in Java projects.
  • Right-click on your project in the Package Explorer pane to create a Java package.
  • Put program files that are usually used together into one package.
    • Because your programs will be small, most of your programs will consist of only one package.
  • Package name rules:
    • Make your package name different from anyone else's package names. Java programmers traditionally use their name, business name, domain name, or e-mail address as the first part of their package names.
    • Use all lowercase letters with no spaces.
    • Use periods between different categories in the package name. For example, if the package name identifies who created the package and what the package will be used for, put a period between the creator and the package's purpose.
  • Java projects are used to organize programs within Eclipse; packages are used to organize programs within Java. Because you're using Eclipse, you'll use both Java projects and packages. If you were to create Java programs without Eclipse, you would probably use only packages.

Create A First Program

Create your first program using the JFrame class as its superclass:

  1. Right-click on your package in the Package Explorer pane and choose New / Class.
  2. Enter HelloWorld for the class name, as shown in the image below. (Hint: there's no space between “Hello” and “World”.)
  3. Click Browse for Superclass.
    1. Enter “jfr” for the type, select JFrame, and click OK.
  4. For Which method stubs(stub) would you like to create?, select only public static void main (String[] args).

  1. Click Finish to create the class.

Eclipse will create code for a HelloWorld class that looks like the following listing.

Listing 0-0, from HelloWorld.java

package annette.godtland.helloworld;
 
import javax.swing.JFrame;
 
public class HelloWorld extends JFrame {
 
  /**
   * @param args
   */
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    // TODO Auto-generated method stub
 
  }
 
}
  1. Remove the comment from above main().
  2. Replace the code in the main() method as indicated in this listing:

Listing 0-1, from HelloWorld.java

package annette.godtland.helloworld;
 
import javax.swing.JFrame;
 
public class HelloWorld extends JFrame {
 
    (Code was removed from here.)
 
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    HelloWorld hello = new HelloWorld();
    hello.setVisible(true);
  }
 
}
  1. Press Ctrl-S to save the program.
  2. Click the Run button, as shown in this image, to run the program:

A tiny window should appear with nothing in it, like this:

The lessons in this book will teach you how to put content into a window.

Key Points and More

  • To create classes, right-click on your package name in the Package Explorer pane.
    • Class names may contain numbers, letters, dollar signs, and underscores. Dollar signs and underscores are usually not used.
    • Blanks or periods aren't allowed in class names.
    • Class names cannot start with a number.
    • Class names typically start with an uppercase letter.
    • If the class name includes more than one word, the first letter of each word is usually uppercase, and the rest of the letters are lowercase.
  • Remove the automatically-generated comments Eclipse creates when you create a class.
  • Press Ctrl-S to save your program.
  • Click the Run button to run your program. The Run button looks like a typical play button.
  • Unless you have syntax errors or are told not to, save and run your program after you make the changes from each code listing. If you have a syntax error, use Quick Fix to fix the error:
    • Rest your mouse on the underlined error in the code. Eclipse will list ways to fix the problem. Select one of the options and Eclipse will fix the error for you.
  • Throughout the lessons, you'll often receive the syntax error that says something couldn't be resolved to a type. If you receive that error, use Quick Fix to import the needed class. The class, along with its package name, will be added to the import statements at the beginning of the file.
  • Code listings may be more difficult to read if lines of text are word wrapped. To reduce word wrapping, set your e-reader to a smaller font.
  • Click the Completed Listing link below any listing to see how to complete the code. However, you may complete the listing differently, if your code does the same thing or if you like what your code does better.
  • The same options won't be used for every class you create. Be sure to follow the instructions exactly as written when you create each class.

Add a Project to the Build Path

The build path holds the location of the projects and libraries needed for creating the program in the Java project. When a program needs to use code that is in a different project or library, the other project or library must be added to the build path of the program's project.

For example, program code that will be shared between multiple programs in this book will be in a separate Java project. The shared project needs to be added to the build path of the project of each program that will use the shared code.

To add additional projects of shared code to a new project as the new project is being created:

  1. Click the Next button.
  2. Click the Projects tab, as shown in the image below.
  3. Click Add....
  4. Select the project to add, then click OK.
  5. Click Finish to finish creating the new project.

To add additional projects of shared code to an existing project:

  1. Right-click on the existing project and select Build Path / Configure Build Path...
  2. Click the Projects tab, as shown in the image above.
  3. Click Add....
  4. Select the project to add, then click OK.
  5. Click OK to close the Java Build Path window.

Export a Program

You must export a finished program if you want to run it without Eclipse or if you want to run it on a different computer.

If you export your program, it will be made into a JAR file (a Java ARchive file) on your computer. JAR files have names that end with “.jar”. To run the program, double-click on the JAR file name.

To export a program:

  1. Right-click on the Java project name in the Package Explorer pane and choose Export.
  2. Select Runnable JAR File, as shown in the image below, and click Next.
  3. Select the launch configuration for your project. Eclipse creates a launch configuration for every new program you run in Eclipse, and adds the launch configuration to this list. The image below shows selecting the launch configuration for the ASCII Art project which was a program created in the first Do-It-Yourself Java Games book.
  4. Enter a name for the JAR file as the Export destination. Naming the JAR file after the Java project will help you remember what program the JAR file contains. The image below shows the JAR file being named ASCIIArt.jar.
  5. Select the option to Package required libraries into generated JAR, as shown in this image:

  1. Click Finish to complete the export.

To run your program without Eclipse:

  1. Find your newly created JAR file in your Java work folder.
  2. Double-click the JAR file name.

You may copy the JAR file to any other folder or any other computer. However, remember to copy any files in the Java work folder that are used by the program, to the same folder as the JAR file.

Key Points and More

  • Export the program as a JAR file if you want to run the program outside of Eclipse or on a different computer.
  • You can save different versions of your program in different JAR files. Use all the same export options but name a different Export destination for each version of the program.
  • Your exported JAR file for the programs created in this book can be run on any computer running a Windows, OS X, or Linux operating system, if a Java Runtime Environment, version 1.7 or later, is installed.
    • The Java Runtime Environment is already installed on most computers, for running other programs.
    • The Java Runtime Environment was included in the Java Development Kit you installed. Therefore, the Java Runtime Environment also was already installed on your computer.
    • Anyone can download and install just the Java Runtime Environment, without the Java Development Kit, from http://java.com/en/download/index.jsp.
  • If there were any files in the Java work folder that were used by the program, always keep a copy of those files in the same folder as the exported JAR file.
  • The JAR file will contain all the .class files that are in the bin folder of the Java work folder. If you want any other files that are in the bin folder inserted into the JAR file, copy them to the src folder before you export the project.

You should now be ready to try the lessons in this book.

Appendix E - Conventions Used and Other Tips

Throughout this book, actions you are to take are given in a numbered list.

Read the Key Points and More at the end of every lesson to review the lesson and to learn a little more. You don't need to memorize them; you can easily refer to them later, if needed. You'll also learn a lot by doing.

Throughout this book, every code listing is shown in a monospaced font between underscored lines.

Code listings may be more difficult to read if text is word wrapped. To reduce word wrapping, set your e-reader to a smaller font.

Above each listing is the file name for the listed code.

Remove from your program any section of code that is shown in the listing as “(Code was removed from here.)”. Also, remove the automatically-generated comments for every class you create. You'll add your own comments in later lessons.

Changes for you to make to your program code are shown in bold in the listings.

Most listings only show a portion of the code from the program file. Each section of code that isn't included in the listing is shown as “...”.

Code that you are to complete yourself is shown in the listings as fill-in blanks, ____________________. Fill in the blanks with zero or more words or symbols.

Click the Completed listing link below any listing if you want to see how to complete the code. However, you'll learn more if you try to complete the code yourself before you look up the answer. You may complete the listing differently, if your code does the same thing or if you like what your code does better.

Use the Appendix A - Glossary as a glossary and an index. The glossary has definitions of programming terms as well as links for where to find more information about the term in the Do-It-Yourself Java Games books.

Bookmark Appendix A - Glossary with your e-reader to more easily get to the glossary.
